title: Group centrality
text:
For many group centrality measures, the problem of finding a group of a given size with maximum centrality can be formulated as an integer linear program.[1,2]

For example, consider the following integer linear program for group degree centrality maximization:

\begin{align}

\text{max} & \quad \sum_{v \in V} y_v \\

\text{s. t.} &\quad

\sum_{v \in V} x_v = k\\

& \forall v \in V: \begin{cases}

x_v+y_v \leq 1 \\

y_v \leq \sum_{u \in N(v)} x_u \\

x_v,y_v \in \{0,1\}

\end{cases}

\end{align}

Here, the x_v variables indicate whether v is in the group, while the y_v variables indicate if v is a non-group neighbor. Thus, the objective function corresponds to C_D(S) = |N(S) \setminus S| , where S = \{v \in V \mid x_v = 1\} . This objective is maximized under the constraint |S| = \sum_{v \in V} x_v = k , as required.

Since it is NP-hard for many group centrality measures to find a subset

### Implementations

The software library NetworkX supports the evaluation of group degree centrality, group closeness and group betweenness, as well as obtaining the most prominent group with respect to group betweenness centrality.[3]

The network analysis toolkit NetworKit supports the evaluation and maximization of group degree centrality, group closeness, group harmonic centrality, group betweenness and more.[4]
